RagShortTexts: The House of Vítkovci bore the five-petaled rose, commanding southern Bohemia under Vok I.

Variants.Content: The Vítkovci were a Slavic noble house of southern Bohemia whose branches carried the red five-petaled rose on their arms. Vok I of Rožmberk, known to German speakers as Rosenberg, led the family's rise by holding the castles of Krumlov and Rožmberk on the upper Vltava. He served as High Marshal of the Kingdom of Bohemia under King Ottokar II, so the family's strength was tied to the Přemyslid crown's wars in Austria and Prussia. The lords of southern Bohemia kept their own estates, courts and fortresses, and that independence made them useful allies but dangerous rivals when the crown tried to centralise power. Their castles controlled the river road, and the tolls from those valleys paid for knights, crossbowmen and the upkeep of stone walls.

A Rožmberk lord knew that royal wars brought both honour and debt. He led Přemyslid hosts into Austria and Prussia, then returned home to defend his baronial liberties against any crown official who tried to collect new taxes or appoint new judges. Each campaign was recorded in the household accounts, and each debt was weighed against the lands that secured it.
The red rose banner flies above Český Krumlov. The lords patronized Cistercian monks at Vyšší Brod, erecting mills and safeguarding rural communities from external tax extortions.
